title: The Half Bowl of Water Beside the Scale
teaser: A little more than two hours before the temple fair opens, Old Yan has injured his wrist, and Xiao Ji must finish several large batches of dough on his own for the first time. The recipe on the wall gives clear weights and times. Only the last half bowl of water beside the scale has no fixed answer that can be given in advance.
paragraphs: At 3:40 a.m., ten jin of flour are already in the basin, and Old Yan’s right wrist is wrapped in a brace. Xiao Ji has worked at the noodle shop for half a year. He is comfortable weighing salt, moving flour, and cutting noodles, and he can recite the card on the wall: base water, salt, resting time, all clearly listed. What Old Yan has always finished himself is the final adjustment of water. Depending on the weather, the flour, and the state of the dough, he sometimes pours in all of it, sometimes only a mouthful, and sometimes leaves the whole bowl untouched. Today he cannot knead for Xiao Ji. For the first time, that last judgment has to rest in Xiao Ji’s own hands.

After mixing in the base amount of water, Xiao Ji grabs a piece of dough. It feels a little dry, so he lifts the half bowl beside the scale. Old Yan does not give him a new number. With his left hand, he pinches off a small piece from the edge of the basin, presses it tight, releases it, and hands it over. Then he asks Xiao Ji to take another piece from the center and make the same comparison. Only after several tries does Xiao Ji begin to distinguish two states that he had previously called by the same words—“a little dry.” One piece breaks along the edge as soon as the pressure is released; the other already holds together, though its surface is still rough. Xiao Ji adds only a small sip of water along the side of the basin.

While the first batch rests, Xiao Ji takes the recipe card down from the wall and tries to record what he has just noticed. He writes “feels right,” stares at it for two seconds, crosses it out, and replaces it with: “Holds together when pressed; no wet strands when released. If the edge breaks as soon as it opens, add water.” Then he looks back through the records from the previous few days. On mornings when the heating was on, the final water adjustment tended to be larger; on rainy days it was smaller, and the resting time shifted slightly too. The hygrometer on the wall reads 54%. Xiao Ji squeezes humidity, final added water, and resting time beneath the original weight figures. For the first time, the card holds both touch and old data.

At 4:25, Xiao Ji finishes the second batch entirely on his own. The dough already holds together, but it is slightly sticky. If he copied the first batch, he would add the same small mouthful of water. He lifts the bowl, then sets it down again and kneads for a little longer. The stickiness gradually fades. He pulls out a test strand; its length and spring are normal. On the edge of the card he adds another line: “Knead longer first, then decide whether stickiness means too little water.” Old Yan sits by the doorway and never touches the basin. Only after Xiao Ji has finished writing does he pass the card back to him.

After daybreak, the steamers and soup pots push the kitchen humidity higher, and the fifth batch also comes from a newly opened sack of flour. According to the earlier numbers, higher humidity seems to suggest less extra water, yet this dough breaks at the edge as soon as it is pressed. Xiao Ji does not force the “high humidity, less water” pattern onto it, and he does not ask Old Yan exactly how much to add today. He follows the actions written on the card—pinch, knead, wait—then adds a little water twice, each time waiting for the dough to absorb it before checking again. Finally, he extends the resting time by three minutes. Old Yan tastes only the first bowl of noodles and never takes over. The fifth batch uses a different amount of water from the second, but Xiao Ji is now judging both through the same set of recognizable cues.

After the lunch rush, Xiao Ji wipes the worktable clean. The original weights are still at the top of the card, but below them are short notes about holding together, cracked edges, stickiness, humidity, and resting time; several floury fingerprints mark the corners. He does not copy it onto a clean “final version.” One last small piece of dough remains beside the scale. He presses it tight, releases it, then looks up at the hygrometer. The needle rests at 68%. He bends down and writes “68%” at the bottom of the card, with a speck of white flour clinging beside the tip of his pen.
concept: SECI describes knowledge as moving and being recreated between tacit and explicit forms. Shared practice allows experience that is difficult to verbalize to be sensed; part of that experience can then be externalized into communicable language or judgment criteria; those expressions can be combined with records, data, and other explicit knowledge; and, through use, the explicit cues can be internalized again as practical capability. The four conversions are not a one-time linear sequence, and they do not translate tacit knowledge completely into an instruction manual.
explanation: The story deliberately removes two simpler explanations: “they were missing the correct recipe” and “Xiao Ji simply became skilled by doing more batches.” The basic weights and times are already explicit, and Xiao Ji has six months of related operating experience, but the final water adjustment changes with the condition of the dough, so Old Yan cannot give one number in advance that will always be correct. The new development begins when they work with the same dough together. Xiao Ji first senses a distinction through shared action, then turns part of that tactile judgment into words that can be shared, combines those words with humidity and historical records, and finally uses, revises, and reabsorbs those cues in independent work. The new flour in the fifth batch deliberately breaks the simple numerical pattern from the earlier batches, showing that what he gains is neither a fixed amount of water nor mere repetition.
mapping: Old Yan and Xiao Ji make the same pressing comparison on dough from the same basin → Experience that is difficult to explain directly first becomes perceptible through shared practice

Short phrases such as “holds together when pressed; no wet strands when released” → Part of the tactile judgment is externalized into a standard that can be discussed and recorded, though it remains incomplete
The tactile phrases are written on the same card as humidity, added water, and resting-time records → New expressions are combined with existing explicit information to create a more useful reference

With new flour in the fifth batch, Xiao Ji can depart from the simple numerical pattern and still judge what to do → Explicit cues are absorbed back into action and continue generating new experience and records
boundary: SECI does not mean that every skill must pass through four stages in a strict order, or that one shared exercise can reproduce expert experience. Knowledge conversion may fail when learners lack basic technique, shared practice is too limited, externalized language is misleading, or records are poor. Highly situated craft still requires continued practice. A recipe card can help experience move between people and forms, but it cannot fully replace skilled judgment.
reflection: When the new flour in the fifth batch breaks the numerical pattern of the earlier batches, what allows Xiao Ji to keep judging instead of asking Old Yan for another number?
